stem: On an average, a human heart is found to beat 75 times in a minute. Calculate its frequency and period.
solution:
The beat frequency of the heart \(= \dfrac{75}{1\,\text{min}} = \dfrac{75}{60\,\text{s}} = 1.25\,\text{s}^{-1} = 1.25\,\text{Hz}\).

The time period \(T = \dfrac{1}{1.25\,\text{s}^{-1}} = 0.8\,\text{s}\).

stem:
Which of the following functions of time represent (a) periodic and (b) non-periodic motion? Give the period for each case of periodic motion [\(\omega\) is any positive constant].

(i) \(\sin \omega t + \cos \omega t\)

(ii) \(\sin \omega t + \cos 2\omega t + \sin 4\omega t\)

(iii) \(e^{-\omega t}\)

(iv) \(\log(\omega t)\)
solution:
(i) \(\sin \omega t + \cos \omega t\) is a periodic function; it can also be written as \(\sqrt{2}\,\sin(\omega t + \pi/4)\).

Now \(\sqrt{2}\,\sin(\omega t + \pi/4) = \sqrt{2}\,\sin(\omega t + \pi/4 + 2\pi) = \sqrt{2}\,\sin\!\left[\omega\left(t + \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}\right) + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\).

The periodic time of the function is \(2\pi/\omega\).

(ii) This is an example of a periodic motion. It can be noted that each term represents a periodic function with a different angular frequency. Since period is the least interval of time after which a function repeats its value, \(\sin \omega t\) has a period \(T_0 = 2\pi/\omega\); \(\cos 2\omega t\) has a period \(\pi/\omega = T_0/2\); and \(\sin 4\omega t\) has a period \(2\pi/4\omega = T_0/4\). The period of the first term is a multiple of the periods of the last two terms. Therefore, the smallest interval of time after which the sum of the three terms repeats is \(T_0\), and thus the sum is a periodic function with a period \(2\pi/\omega\).

(iii) The function \(e^{-\omega t}\) is not periodic, it decreases monotonically with increasing time and tends to zero as \(t \to \infty\) and thus, never repeats its value.

(iv) The function \(\log(\omega t)\) increases monotonically with time \(t\). It, therefore, never repeats its value and is a non-periodic function. It may be noted that as \(t \to \infty\), \(\log(\omega t)\) diverges to \(\infty\). It, therefore, cannot represent any kind of physical displacement.

stem:
Which of the following functions of time represent (a) simple harmonic motion and (b) periodic but not simple harmonic? Give the period for each case.

(1) \(\sin \omega t - \cos \omega t\)

(2) \(\sin^2 \omega t\)
solution:
(a) \(\sin \omega t - \cos \omega t\)

\(= \sin \omega t - \sin(\pi/2 - \omega t)\)

\(= 2\cos(\pi/4)\,\sin(\omega t - \pi/4)\)

\(= \sqrt{2}\,\sin(\omega t - \pi/4)\)

This function represents a simple harmonic motion having a period \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) and a phase angle \((-\pi/4)\) or \((7\pi/4)\).

(b) \(\sin^2 \omega t\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2\omega t\)

The function is periodic having a period \(T = \pi/\omega\). It also represents a harmonic motion with the point of equilibrium occurring at \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) instead of zero.
_note: The book labels the two functions (1) and (2) in the question but answers them as (a) and (b). Transcribed as printed.

context: The two circular motions referred to are: (a) a circle of radius \(A\) with period \(T = 4\,\text{s}\), the particle P starting at \(t = 0\) on a radius that makes \(45^\circ\) with the positive \(x\)-axis, revolving anticlockwise; and (b) a circle of radius \(B\) with period \(T = 30\,\text{s}\), the particle P starting at \(t = 0\) on the positive \(y\)-axis, revolving clockwise.
stem: The figure given below depicts two circular motions. The radius of the circle, the period of revolution, the initial position and the sense of revolution are indicated in the figures. Obtain the simple harmonic motions of the \(x\)-projection of the radius vector of the rotating particle P in each case.
solution:
(a) At \(t = 0\), OP makes an angle of \(45^\circ = \pi/4\) rad with the (positive direction of) \(x\)-axis. After time \(t\), it covers an angle \(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}t\) in the anticlockwise sense, and makes an angle of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) with the \(x\)-axis.

The projection of OP on the \(x\)-axis at time \(t\) is given by

\(x(t) = A\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)

For \(T = 4\,\text{s}\),

\(x(t) = A\cos\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{4}t + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\)

which is a SHM of amplitude \(A\), period \(4\,\text{s}\), and an initial phase \(= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

(b) In this case at \(t = 0\), OP makes an angle of \(90^\circ = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) with the \(x\)-axis. After a time \(t\), it covers an angle of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}t\) in the clockwise sense and makes an angle of \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{2\pi}{T}t\right)\) with the \(x\)-axis. The projection of OP on the \(x\)-axis at time \(t\) is given by

\(x(t) = B\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{2\pi}{T}t\right) = B\sin\!\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{T}t\right)\)

For \(T = 30\,\text{s}\),

\(x(t) = B\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t\right)\)

Writing this as \(x(t) = B\cos\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{15}t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\), and comparing with Eq. (13.4), we find that this represents a SHM of amplitude \(B\), period \(30\,\text{s}\), and an initial phase of \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

subtopic: Velocity, Acceleration and Force Law in SHM
stem:
A body oscillates with SHM according to the equation (in SI units),

\(x = 5\cos\left[2\pi t + \pi/4\right]\).

At \(t = 1.5\,\text{s}\), calculate the (a) displacement, (b) speed and (c) acceleration of the body.
solution:
The angular frequency \(\omega\) of the body \(= 2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1}\) and its time period \(T = 1\,\text{s}\).

At \(t = 1.5\,\text{s}\)

(a) displacement \(= (5.0\,\text{m})\cos\left[(2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1}) \times 1.5\,\text{s} + \pi/4\right]\)

\(= (5.0\,\text{m})\cos\left[(3\pi + \pi/4)\right]\)

\(= -5.0 \times 0.707\,\text{m} = -3.535\,\text{m}\)

(b) Using Eq. (13.9), the speed of the body

\(= -(5.0\,\text{m})(2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1})\sin\left[(2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1}) \times 1.5\,\text{s} + \pi/4\right]\)

\(= -(5.0\,\text{m})(2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1})\sin\left[(3\pi + \pi/4)\right]\)

\(= 10\pi \times 0.707\,\text{m s}^{-1} = 22\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

(c) Using Eq. (13.10), the acceleration of the body

\(= -(2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1})^2 \times\) displacement

\(= -(2\pi\,\text{s}^{-1})^2 \times (-3.535\,\text{m})\)

\(= 140\,\text{m s}^{-2}\)

context: In Fig. 13.14 the block of mass \(m\) rests on a horizontal surface between two fixed vertical supports, with one spring of spring constant \(k\) joining it to the support on its left and an identical spring joining it to the support on its right.
stem: Two identical springs of spring constant \(k\) are attached to a block of mass \(m\) and to fixed supports as shown in Fig. 13.14. Show that when the mass is displaced from its equilibrium position on either side, it executes a simple harmonic motion. Find the period of oscillations.
solution:
Let the mass be displaced by a small distance \(x\) to the right side of the equilibrium position, as shown in Fig. 13.15. Under this situation the spring on the left side gets elongated by a length equal to \(x\) and that on the right side gets compressed by the same length. The forces acting on the mass are then,

\(F_1 = -kx\) (force exerted by the spring on the left side, trying to pull the mass towards the mean position)

\(F_2 = -kx\) (force exerted by the spring on the right side, trying to push the mass towards the mean position)

The net force, \(F\), acting on the mass is then given by,

\(F = -2kx\)

Hence the force acting on the mass is proportional to the displacement and is directed towards the mean position; therefore, the motion executed by the mass is simple harmonic. The time period of oscillations is,

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{2k}}\)

stem: A block whose mass is \(1\,\text{kg}\) is fastened to a spring. The spring has a spring constant of \(50\,\text{N m}^{-1}\). The block is pulled to a distance \(x = 10\,\text{cm}\) from its equilibrium position at \(x = 0\) on a frictionless surface from rest at \(t = 0\). Calculate the kinetic, potential and total energies of the block when it is \(5\,\text{cm}\) away from the mean position.
solution:
The block executes SHM, its angular frequency, as given by Eq. (13.14b), is

\(\omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{50\,\text{N m}^{-1}}{1\,\text{kg}}} = 7.07\,\text{rad s}^{-1}\)

Its displacement at any time \(t\) is then given by,

\(x(t) = 0.1\cos(7.07\,t)\)

Therefore, when the particle is \(5\,\text{cm}\) away from the mean position, we have

\(0.05 = 0.1\cos(7.07\,t)\)

Or \(\cos(7.07\,t) = 0.5\) and hence

\(\sin(7.07\,t) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 0.866\)

Then, the velocity of the block at \(x = 5\,\text{cm}\) is

\(= 0.1 \times 7.07 \times 0.866\,\text{m s}^{-1} = 0.61\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Hence the K.E. of the block,

\(= \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[1\,\text{kg} \times (0.6123\,\text{m s}^{-1})^2\right] = 0.19\,\text{J}\)

The P.E. of the block,

\(= \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(50\,\text{N m}^{-1} \times 0.05\,\text{m} \times 0.05\,\text{m}) = 0.0625\,\text{J}\)

The total energy of the block at \(x = 5\,\text{cm}\),

\(=\) K.E. \(+\) P.E. \(= 0.25\,\text{J}\)

We also know that at maximum displacement, K.E. is zero and hence the total energy of the system is equal to the P.E. Therefore, the total energy of the system,

\(= \tfrac{1}{2}(50\,\text{N m}^{-1} \times 0.1\,\text{m} \times 0.1\,\text{m}) = 0.25\,\text{J}\)

which is same as the sum of the two energies at a displacement of \(5\,\text{cm}\). This is in conformity with the principle of conservation of energy.
_note: Printed defect: the book's velocity line prints "= 0.1 x 7.07  0.866 m s-1" with the second multiplication sign dropped; restored here. The book then states that velocity as 0.61 m s-1 but substitutes 0.6123 m s-1 into the K.E. line - both retained as printed.

stem: What is the length of a simple pendulum, which ticks seconds?
solution:
From Eq. (13.26), the time period of a simple pendulum is given by,

\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{g}}\)

From this relation one gets,

\(L = \dfrac{gT^2}{4\pi^2}\)

The time period of a simple pendulum, which ticks seconds, is \(2\,\text{s}\). Therefore, for \(g = 9.8\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) and \(T = 2\,\text{s}\), \(L\) is

\(= \dfrac{9.8\,(\text{m s}^{-2}) \times 4\,(\text{s}^2)}{4\pi^2} = 1\,\text{m}\)

(a) A swimmer completing one (return) trip from one bank of a river to the other and back.

(b) A freely suspended bar magnet displaced from its N-S direction and released.

(c) A hydrogen molecule rotating about its centre of mass.

(d) An arrow released from a bow.

Which of the following examples represent (nearly) simple harmonic motion and which represent periodic but not simple harmonic motion?

(a) the rotation of earth about its axis.

(b) motion of an oscillating mercury column in a U-tube.

(c) motion of a ball bearing inside a smooth curved bowl, when released from a point slightly above the lower most point.

(d) general vibrations of a polyatomic molecule about its equilibrium position.
Fig. 13.18 depicts four \(x\)-\(t\) plots for linear motion of a particle. Which of the plots represent periodic motion? What is the period of motion (in case of periodic motion)?
